newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 10.

text.p: Cyclone Drena, the second to hit northern New Zealand in 10 days, was bearing down on Northland on Thursday night, with MetService predicting two possible paths as it heads south. Chief meteorologist Augie Auer said the cyclone could track over Taranaki, Wanganui and Wairarapa or take a more western track over Taranaki and head straight for Nelson. The cyclone is expected to hit the top of the North Island this morning. Page 1.

International Trade Minister Lockwood Smith on Thursday described as "gravely disappointing" and "a step backward" a United States decision to start subsidising its butter exports and to step up skim milk powder subsidies. The decision could see up to 39,000 tonnes of butterfat dumped on world markets, with a downward effect on New Zealand farmers' prices. Page 2.

The Education Ministry holds record cards for 2,832 school-age children who appear "lost" inside or outside the education system. A review two years ago recommended establishing an electronic database to ensure that children who

left a school were re-enrolled somewhere else. But the recommendation has not been acted on. Labour education spokesman Trevor Mallard on Thursday provided figures that said the Education Ministry held 2,832 cards, which gave the only official indication of the extent of long-term truancy. Page 2.

The public is not interested in hearing about the "dirty washing" of NZ First or other political parties, according to NZ First MP and Police Minister Jack Elder. He was responding to the news that ACT NZ has hired former NZ First staffer Rex Widerstrom to write a paper on the secret workings of his former
party. "Good luck to them," Elder said on Thursday. Page 2.

A Commerce Ministry investigation into the collapse of Kiwi International Airlines had found evidence of mismanagement and breaches of the Companies Act which could lead to court action, ministry solicitor Adam Feeley said on Thursday. He said the ministry's investigation had completed an "exhaustive" inquiry into the affairs of the budget airline, which collapsed in September with debts of $5 million. Page 3.

Building industry shares have soared on the back of promises of increased government spending. Shares in four leading building companies have all leapt to record highs since the October general election. During the past three months Fletcher Challenge Building shares have hit a record high of $4.62, Steel and Tube Holdings have reached a high of $9.30, Richina Pacific achieved a four-year high of 54 cents and Milburn New Zealand climbed to a 15-month high of $3.32. The government said it would spend an extra $5 billion between 1997 and 2000. Page 12.

Brierley Investments' ringfencing of its controlling Air New Zealand stake into a New Zealand subsidiary was not a precedent for other foreign-owned companies to get around Overseas Investment Commission requirements, the commission said. The commission had removed BIL from its second schedule list, which exempts companies from its regulations. The list includes companies with more than 25 percent foreign ownership but still in New Zealand hands. Page 12.

Cerebos Gregg is pouring all its juice drinks into a joint venture with Rio Beverages. Under the deal announced on Thursday the stocks, assets, and goodwill of both companies will go into the joint venture, to be run at Rio's plant in East Tamaki. General manager will be Rio head David Thexton. The new entity will have an estimated turnover of $32 million a year. Page 12.

Telecom has begun selling its loss-making Australian subsidiary Pacific Star, with the sale of Pacific Star Mobile to CXA Communications for A$4.5 million. Telecom communications manager Linda Sanders confirmed on Thursday that the remainder
of Pacific Star would be sold. Page 12.

Media moguls Rupert Murdoch and Kerry Packer are understood to have had a meeting in the Bay of Islands shortly before New Year. Analysts believe it is the first time the two have met since London in November 1995. Observers say topics of discussion between the two in the Bay of Islands were likely to have included the possibility of reuniting the Super League and Australian Rugby League branches, the ownership of Fairfax Group (publisher of the Sydney Morning Herald and The Age), and a dispute over rights to Murdoch-owned Fox Television programmes.
